newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Sprint invests to keep customers.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Sprint invests to keep customers.

text.p: Sprint Corp has invested tens of millions of dollars to cut down the proportion of its small business customers who leave for other carriers -- known in the industry as churn -- and says it is working.

"We have seen a 33 percent increase in small business customer loyalty year over year, which is unprecedented for us and probably industry leading," Patti Manuel, president of sales and marketing for Sprint Business, told Reuters.
The company derived 15-25 pct of its $14 billion 1996 revenues from small business, depending on calculation method.

Sprint has built a customer business center in Louisville, Kentucky, which has 250 consultants who get to know customers and their business needs. The center has been active for a year, though was only formally launched six months ago.

"I would view it as a large upfront expense which pays for itself over time," she said in an interview. The company said it spent $35 million on the center in 1996 on top of some resources switched there from other support efforts.
Winning customers in the highly competitive telecom industry is very expensive, with advertising, marketing and promotion costs which can take many months to recover.

If a customer is lost to a rival after a few months, the carrier is sitting on a heavy loss. So most carriers like AT&T Corp, MCI Communications Corp and Sprint are working harder at keeping customers than getting new ones.
Manuel declined to give the actual rate of customer turnover, but said benefits have been not only more durable relationships with customers, but a majority taking more than one Sprint product.
The time needed to help customers gradually falls as Sprint knows more about its customers, a process helped by a large database at the center.
"What we are really struggling with a bit is what is important to our small business customer," she said.
Though industry models predict customers most want services all provided on a single bill, Manuel said that was not always the case for her small business users.
"In most customer cases getting the problem resolved at a single point of contact is more important," she said.
Having the Global One alliance with France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom AG has given an extra dimension to Sprint's marketing punch.
"The Global One alliance has enabled us to penetrate U.S. business which is not headquartered here," she said.
"Likewise we have helped them from a defensive perspective in their countries with a lot of U.S.-based companies too," Manuel said.
One surprising development has been the slow take up of Internet services by small business customers, only 20 percent of whom are users.

"(That is) not as fast as we would like," she said, adding that one reason may be a dearth of applications-based packages of Internet services. This would tie in Internet use to a particular business advantage, like business to business information or directories. ((-- New York Newsrom 212 859 1610))
